issues.legal_issue: The State must provide effective rehabilitation to bonded labourers after their release, and failure to do so violates their constitutional rights.
material_facts: About 135 bonded labourers had been released and returned to their villages following an earlier court order.
More than 18 months later, most had not received rehabilitation assistance and were living without land or work and near starvation.
The State had promised rehabilitation but could not establish that the released labourers had in fact been rehabilitated.
issues.conclusion: The State was directed to provide suitable rehabilitative assistance to the 135 released labourers, with the assistance determined by the vigilance committee and provided in the presence of a social action group representative.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 21 and 23 of the Constitution require bonded labourers to be identified and released and, upon release, suitably rehabilitated. The Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976 provides for rehabilitation; merely freeing workers without effective rehabilitation frustrates the Act and may drive them back into bondage.

issues.definition: When a public-interest writ concerns bonded labourers who have been released but not effectively assisted, the State must provide suitable rehabilitation.

issues.legal_issue: Forced labour for no remuneration or nominal remuneration gives rise to a presumption that the worker is a bonded labourer unless the presumption is rebutted by satisfactory material.
material_facts: The State’s officials appeared to require proof of an advance or other economic consideration before treating a worker as bonded.
The Court relied on its earlier decision explaining that a worker providing forced labour may be unable to prove the circumstances of bondage through a formal adversarial process.
The Court directed the State to apply the presumption when identifying bonded labourers.
issues.conclusion: Whenever a worker is found to be providing forced labour for no or nominal remuneration, the State must treat the worker as a bonded labourer unless the employer or the State produces satisfactory material rebutting that presumption.
issues.legal_principle: Under the test stated in Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India, proof that a worker is made to provide forced labour raises a presumption that the worker does so in consideration of an advance or other economic consideration and is therefore a bonded labourer under the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976. The presumption may be rebutted by the employer or the State with satisfactory material; a formal trial-like proof requirement must not obstruct identification and relief.

issues.definition: When a bonded-labour public-interest writ concerns forced labour for no or nominal wages and no satisfactory rebuttal is produced, the worker is presumed to be a bonded labourer.

issues.legal_issue: Grassroots social action groups should be involved in vigilance and identification work when official efforts to identify bonded labourers are ineffective.
material_facts: The State reported very low numbers of bonded labourers identified, released, and rehabilitated, and its vigilance committees appeared ineffective.
The Court observed that workers might be afraid to disclose their circumstances when questioned by officials in the presence of landlords.
Social action groups were working among poor and vulnerable communities and could help identify bonded labourers.
The Court directed the State to include specified social action group representatives in local vigilance committees and to involve representatives who reported bonded labour in identification visits.
issues.conclusion: The State was directed to include social action group representatives in the relevant vigilance committees and, when a representative reports bonded labour, to take immediate identification and release steps, include the representative in the visit, and provide that representative with a copy of the resulting report.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13 of the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976 provides for vigilance committees. The Court held that committees and official machinery should be made effective by involving grassroots social action groups, whose work can help reveal bondage that workers may be unable or afraid to report to officials acting alone.
